summary: This unit teaches you to sell the products and services of a salon or spa honestly and well: know what you sell, find out what each client needs, explain features and benefits, link one sale to another, handle price worries and buying signals, close the sale, and follow up. You will also learn to set up a clean, safe retail display, run a simple promotion, sell within the law and record sales against targets.

blocks.p: Every salon and spa lives on two kinds of income: services (a cut, a facial, a pedicure) and products (the shampoo, cream or nail oil the client takes home). Selling is not a separate job done by a pushy salesperson. It is a natural part of caring for the client: you find out what she needs, and you offer the product or service that will help. This unit is for COSMETOLOGY LEVEL 2 trainees and applies in a hair salon, a nail bar or a day spa.

Good selling is **honest, helpful and polite**. A client who buys something that suits her comes back and tells her friends. A client who is pressured into something she does not need, or is told something untrue, does not return. So this unit is about listening and advice as much as about persuasion.

blocks.note: How you are assessed: theory papers (multiple-choice questions, short answers and essays, including some sums in J$) and practical role plays and a display in the Centre's reception or salon. The assessor watches your greeting, questions, honest advice, hygiene with testers and the way you close and record a sale.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.note: In practical work, photograph hands, products and paperwork. Never photograph a client's or model's face unless she agrees and the Centre allows it.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: You cannot advise a client about something you do not understand. Client trust begins with correct answers. If you are not sure, say so and find out; a wrong answer is worse than 'let me check for you'.

head: Kind
What it is
Examples
rows: Retail products
Sold to clients to use at home.
Shampoo, conditioner, leave-in, edge control, cuticle oil, hand cream, sunscreen, body butter, nail polish
Professional (back-bar) products
Used by staff on clients during services; not usually sold.
Large tubs of relaxer, hair colour, peroxide, salon-size shampoo, wax, massage oil

ul: **The label:** name, what it does, directions, ingredients, warnings, batch number, expiry date, size and maker.
**The maker's leaflet or website** and the salon's product training.
**The safety data sheet (SDS)** for chemical products: hazards, safe storage and first aid. It is for staff, not a sales document.
**Your senior stylist or supervisor.** Ask when you do not know.
Try the products yourself where the salon allows, and note how they feel and smell.

head: On the label
What it tells you
rows: Directions for use
How much, how often and where to apply it.
Ingredients list
What is in it, written in order from the most to the least. Check it for anything the client is allergic to.
Expiry date or open-jar symbol
The date after which it should not be sold or used. A picture of an open jar with a number and an M (for example '12M') means use within that many months after opening.
SPF number (sunscreen)
SPF means sun protection factor: how well it protects against the rays that burn. A higher number gives more protection but no sunscreen blocks everything; it must be reapplied.
Warnings
Patch test needed? Keep out of the eyes? Not for use on broken skin?

blocks.p: For every service on the price list, be able to tell a client: **what it involves, how long it takes, what it costs, and any preparation or aftercare**. Know which services should be preceded by a skin (patch) test, which are not suitable for some clients, and which products link well with each service. If a client asks about a service in another part of the business (for example a hair stylist asked about nails), introduce her to the colleague who knows most.
A **feature** is a fact about the product itself. A **benefit** is what that fact does for the client. People buy benefits.

head: Product
Feature (the fact)
Benefit (what it does for her)
rows: Leave-in conditioner
Contains shea butter and glycerin
Keeps dry hair soft and easy to comb, so it breaks less
Sunscreen
SPF 30; oil-free
Helps protect your face from sunburn and does not leave oily skin shiny
Cuticle oil
Comes in a small bottle with a brush
You can keep it in your bag and dress your cuticles each day, so they stay soft
Satin bonnet
Smooth satin inside
Does not soak up moisture or rub the hair, so your style lasts longer and your hair stays moist

blocks.note: Say the benefit in words that link to what the client told you: 'You said your ends are dry and break. This leave-in keeps them soft, so you will see less breakage.' Start with her need, not with the product's list of ingredients.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.h: Skin, hair and nail basics for recommending

head: Client's need
What you notice
Suitable product family
rows: Dry hair or scalp
Rough, dull, breaks; tight, flaky scalp
Moisturising shampoo and conditioner, leave-in, scalp oil
Oily scalp or hair
Greasy shine soon after washing
Shampoo for oily hair; light conditioner on the ends only
Chemically treated hair (relaxer, colour)
Weaker, more porous
Gentle shampoo and conditioner for treated hair; protein and moisture treatments as the hair needs
Natural, coily hair
Dry lengths, shrinkage, tangles
Moisturising conditioner, leave-in, detangling products, satin bonnet
Oily skin
Shiny all over; large, open pores
Gel or light lotion cleansers, oil-free moisturiser
Dry skin
Tight, flaky, dull
Cream cleanser, rich moisturiser
Sun-exposed skin
Burns easily, dark marks
Sunscreen; after-sun lotion
Dry cuticles and nails
Cracked, peeling cuticles; brittle nails
Cuticle oil, hand cream, strengthening base coat
Cracked heels
Hard, dry skin
Foot cream, a paraffin wax or heel treatment

blocks.note: Do not diagnose a skin or scalp condition, and do not sell a product to 'treat' an infection or disease. If the skin looks sore, infected or unusual, suggest she sees a doctor or pharmacist.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: The most common mistake in selling is to start talking about a product before you know what the client needs. Always **ask and listen first**. A client who feels heard trusts your advice; a client who feels 'sold to' does not.

ul: Greet the client within a moment of her arrival: smile, make eye contact, say 'Good morning' or 'Good afternoon' and use her name if you know it.
Be neat and well groomed: clients trust advice from a person who looks clean and professional. Clean hands and uniform, hair tidy, no strong perfume.
Speak clearly and at the client's level, without jargon. A Jamaican client may be most comfortable in Standard English or Patois; follow her lead politely, and never talk down.

head: Type
What it does
Example
rows: Open question
Starts with how, what, why, tell me about. Gets the client talking about her needs.
'How do you care for your hair at home?' 'What would you like to change about your skin?'
Closed question
Can be answered yes or no. Useful to check facts.
'Are you allergic to anything?' 'Do you use a heat tool?'

flow: Check her record card (past services, purchases, allergies)
Ask open questions about her home care and wishes
Listen without interrupting
Repeat the main points back to check you understood
Look at the hair, skin or nails and judge the type and condition
Ask about allergies, budget and time
Recommend one or two products that match what she said

blocks.h: What to listen and look for

ul: **Words:** 'my ends keep breaking', 'my skin feels tight', 'I never have time'.
**Condition:** dry ends, oily T-zone, peeling cuticles, product build-up.
**Lifestyle:** swims in the sea, works in the sun, wears her hair under a wig, has little time in the morning.
**Budget:** she may tell you, or show you by what she picks up. Never judge what she can afford.
**Allergies and skin problems:** ask every time, even when you ask regularly.

blocks.note: A client says her hair breaks easily. Do not reach for the strongest-sounding product. Ask how she styles and treats her hair and look at its condition first: breakage can come from heat, tight styles, relaxers or lack of moisture, and each needs different advice.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: A **buying signal** is something a client says or does that shows she is interested in buying. When you see one, stop explaining and move towards closing the sale.

head: Signal
Example
rows: She handles the product
Picks up the tester, smells it, reads the label
She asks questions about use and price
'How long does a bottle last?' 'How much is it?'
She compares sizes or other items
'Is there a smaller one?'
She talks about owning it
'This would be good for my daughter too.'
She nods, smiles, relaxes
Her body language opens up

blocks.note: Silence and a frown are signals too. If she steps back, folds her arms or looks away, slow down and ask what worries her.
blocks.label: Remember

sections.title: Recommending, linking and adding to the sale

ul: Recommend **one or two** products that fit what she told you. Too many choices confuse her.
Say why each one suits her, using a benefit that links to her need.
Say how to use it, how much and how often, and how long a bottle lasts.
Mention the price in J$ clearly and honestly, and any offer that is running.
Let her try a tester (see the next section). Then ask if she has any questions.

blocks.p: **Link selling** (linked selling) means suggesting an item that goes with what the client is already having or buying. It works because it helps her get a better result and makes her visit worth more.

head: Service she is having
Linked product or service
Why it helps her
rows: Relaxer or colour
Gentle shampoo and conditioner for chemically treated hair; a deep conditioning treatment
Treated hair is weaker and needs moisture and protein at home
Deep conditioning treatment
Leave-in conditioner; satin bonnet
Keeps the moisture in after she leaves
Braids or weave
Scalp oil; diluted shampoo bottle; satin scarf
Keeps the scalp clean and the style neat
Manicure
Cuticle oil; hand cream; top coat
Keeps cuticles soft and polish from chipping
Pedicure
Foot cream; a paraffin wax foot treatment
Softens dry heels and extends the treatment
Facial
Cleanser, moisturiser or sunscreen for her skin type
Keeps skin healthy between visits
Body scrub or massage
Body lotion or butter; a package with another treatment
Keeps the skin soft

blocks.note: Link suggestions come from the consultation, not from what the salon wants to clear. If the suggestion does not match a need she told you, do not make it.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: **Upselling** means offering a better, larger or fuller version of what the client is already buying, for example the large size that costs less per ml, or adding a conditioning treatment to a wash and set. It is honest only when the better version really gives her more value.

head: Offer
What it is
Example
rows: Package deal
Several services sold together for less than they cost separately.
A 'Relax Package': massage and facial together for less than the two cost alone.
Bundle
Products sold together at one price.
Shampoo, conditioner and leave-in set.
Percentage discount
A part of the price taken off.
25% off a conditioner.
Buy some, get one free
A free item with a purchase.
Buy two gels, get the third free.
Free sample or gift with purchase
A small free item to try.
A trial-size serum with a facial.
Gift voucher
A voucher for a set value, bought as a gift.
A J$8,000 spa voucher.
Loyalty offer
A reward for repeat visits.
A free treatment after ten visits.

blocks.p: Work every sum twice, and show the client the price before and after the offer.

head: Offer
How to work it out
Worked example
rows: 25% off
Divide by 4 (or: 10% = divide by 10, then add up). Take it off the price.
20% off
Divide by 5.
J$1,500 / 5 = J$300 off. Sale price J$1,200.
10% off
Divide by 10.
Buy 2, get the third free
Pay for two only.
3 gels at J$950 each: pay 2 x J$950 = **J$1,900**.
Package saving
Add the separate prices; subtract the package price.
Massage J$5,000 + facial J$6,000 = J$11,000; package J$9,500; she saves J$1,500.

blocks.note: GCT (general consumption tax) is added to the price of most goods and services at the current rate set by law, and the till is usually set up to do it. Never work from a rate you have memorised: use the rate the salon gives you.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.h: Testers: let her try it hygienically

blocks.p: Clients buy what they can smell, touch and see. A tester is an open sample for trying. It must be clean and safe, because many people use it.

ul: Choose **pump bottles** or tubs used with a **clean, single-use spatula**. Never let clients dip their fingers into a tub, and never double-dip a spatula.
Mark testers clearly as 'tester', and never sell the tester itself.
Ask about **allergies** before a product touches the skin. Do not apply a tester to broken, sore or irritated skin, and keep it away from the eyes.
Wash or sanitise your hands before and after handling testers.
Check testers every day: remove any that have changed colour or smell, are dirty or past their date.
Samples to take home go in a clean, labelled, sealed container.

blocks.note: A tester tub with fingerprints and hair in it is an infection risk and makes the whole salon look dirty. Replace it, do not wipe it and carry on.
blocks.label: Safety

head: Do
Why
rows: Place it where clients can see it, such as near reception, but clear of walkways, doors and the fire exit.
Visible, and safe in an emergency.
Keep it out of direct sun and heat, for example not in a hot shop window.
Heat and sunlight can spoil products and fade the labels. Jamaica's heat can make creams separate and bottles leak.
Clean the shelves and wipe each product before setting it out.
A clean display shows the salon is clean.
Put heavy items and glass bottles on the lower shelves.
Safer to lift and cannot fall on someone.
Group products by need or type (hair, skin, nails) with labels facing forward.
Clients find what they want.
Show a clear price ticket in J$ on every item, and the offer and end date on a sign.
Clients know the cost before they ask.
Put older stock at the front and new stock behind (first in, first out).
The older stock sells before it expires.
Keep it well lit and easy to reach.
Clean, well-lit shelves with prices shown sell best.
Check, clean and top up every day before the salon opens; remove damaged, leaking or out-of-date items.
A tidy, full display looks professional and is safe.

flow: Check the stock is in date and in good condition
Set a goal and a time (for example 20 jars in four weeks)
Choose a fair offer
Build a clear display with prices and an end date
Teach every staff member the features and benefits
Tell clients: signs, word of mouth, social media, messages to clients who agreed to receive them
Count the sales against the goal and decide whether to repeat it

ul: A promotion must be **honest**: the price, the end date and any conditions are clear, and the 'was' price is the real earlier price.
Make sure staff can supply what is advertised; do not promote what you cannot supply.
Do not promote products that are out of date or near their expiry just to get rid of them.

blocks.note: Use clients' phone numbers and photographs only with their permission. Keep the list private and let anyone who asks to stop receiving messages do so at once.
blocks.label: Jamaica

sections.title: Handling doubts and closing the sale

blocks.p: An **objection** is a reason the client gives for not buying yet, such as the price, 'I already have something', or 'I need to think'. It is not a rejection: it is information. Listen without arguing, agree that her concern is fair, then answer it honestly.

head: What she says
What she may mean
A good reply
rows: 'That serum is too dear.'
It costs more than she planned; she is not sure of the value.
'I understand. One bottle lasts about two months, so it is only a little each week. There is a smaller size if you would like to try it first.'
'I already have a conditioner.'
She does not see a need.
'What do you like about it? This one is made for relaxed hair and you told me your ends are dry. May I show you the difference?'
'I want to think about it.'
She needs time, or she is not convinced.
'Of course. May I write the products down for you, and give you a leaflet? You are welcome to come back.'
'I cannot afford it today.'
True, or she is polite.
'No problem at all. Here is a small sample to try, and a leaflet. You can buy it on your next visit.'
'Will it really work?'
She has been disappointed before.
'It should help your hair feel softer, but no product works overnight. Use it as directed and tell me how you get on.'

flow: Listen without interrupting
Agree that her worry is reasonable
Answer with true facts (value, size, how long it lasts)
Offer a choice (smaller size, cheaper product, sample, buy later)
Accept her answer politely

blocks.note: Never pressure a client. Pushing makes her feel uncomfortable, damages trust in the salon and can amount to unfair selling. One happy client who buys next month is worth more than one forced sale today. Note her interest on her record so you can mention it another time.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: **Closing the sale** means getting the client's agreement to buy and completing the payment. When you see buying signals, ask in a polite, easy way.

ul: **Direct:** 'Would you like to take the shampoo and the conditioner today?'
**Easy:** 'Shall I put the shampoo and the conditioner with your bill?'
**Choice:** 'Would you like the large bottle or the small one?'

blocks.p: If she says yes, take payment (see the unit on financial transactions), give a **receipt**, and put the product in a bag. If she says no, thank her and smile.

ul: Tell her **how to use** the product, **how much** to use and **how to store** it (cool, dry, lid closed, out of the sun).
Write the products she bought on her **client record card**, so any staff member can give good advice and suggest refills next time.
Agree a **follow-up** if she would like one: for example, the therapist phones two weeks later to ask how the skin care set is working. This shows care, and fixes problems early.
Thank her by name and invite her back.

blocks.note: If a client brings a product back because it has gone bad or caused a problem, listen, apologise, check the receipt and the product, and follow the salon's returns policy. Offer a replacement or refund as the policy allows, and tell your supervisor.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Selling honestly, safely and within the law

ul: **Never make false claims.** A cream cannot remove stretch marks for good, regrow lost hair or cure a disease unless the maker truthfully says so. Say what the maker claims and no more: 'It may help your skin feel softer.'
Do not say a competitor's product is bad. Talk about what yours does.
Do not pretend a product is 'nearly sold out' or 'the last one' when it is not.
Admit when you do not know. Find out, or ask a senior.

blocks.h: A client's rights when she buys

head: Right
What it means in the salon
rows: True information
Product facts and advice are correct; no false claims about results.
Clear prices
Prices are shown on products and on the service price list, so she knows the cost before she agrees. GCT is added at the current rate as the law requires.
A receipt
She is given a receipt showing the date, items, prices, any GCT and the total.
Safe, in-date goods
Products are in date, sealed and stored properly.
A fair remedy
If a product is faulty or not as described, she may bring it back with her receipt and be offered a replacement, repair or refund, following the salon's policy and consumer protection law.
Privacy
Her record and purchases are kept private.

blocks.p: In Jamaica, a shopper who has been treated unfairly or sold faulty goods can contact the **Consumer Affairs Commission**. Following honest practice in the salon makes that rarely necessary.

ul: Ask about allergies before you recommend or apply anything. A client allergic to nuts must not be sold a body butter containing nut oils such as almond oil: **read the ingredients list**.
For chemical services such as hair colour or a lash tint, tell the client that a **skin (patch) test** is needed first, often 48 hours before, as the maker requires, and note the result.
Tell her what a reaction looks like (redness, itching, swelling, burning) and what to do: rinse off, stop using it, and get medical advice.
If a client asks about a product or service in an area you do not know, introduce her to the colleague who does.
Do not offer medical advice or recommend products for medical conditions. Refer to a doctor or pharmacist.
Do not give a discount that is not on the price list or offers. Ask the manager or owner, who decides within the salon's policy.

blocks.note: Keep prices, offers and returns rules in one place that every staff member can read, so clients get the same answer from everyone.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.h: Why a salon records its sales

ul: To see **what sells well and what sells slowly**, so the salon orders enough of the popular items and does not buy more of what sits on the shelf until it expires.
To measure each staff member's sales against **targets** and work out any commission.
To help clients: a note of what she bought lets staff give good advice and remind her when a refill is due.
To handle returns, and to check the till and the stock at the end of the day.

blocks.p: A **target** is a sales figure a staff member or the salon aims for in a set time. **Commission** is an extra payment, often a part of the sales the worker makes. Both must be fair and clear in writing, and they must never push staff into pressuring clients.

head: Example
Working
rows: Target J$30,000 in a month; Tanisha has sold J$22,500. How much more?
Three clients buy J$4,500, J$2,750 and J$6,000 of products. Total?
Target 20 jars in 4 weeks; 8 sold in week 1. How many a week for the rest?
12 left / 3 weeks = 4 a week.
Commission of 5% on J$40,000 sales

head: Record
What it shows
rows: Sales slip or till receipt
Each sale: date, items, prices, GCT, total.
Daily sales record
Total sales for the day by staff member and product.
Client record card
What each client bought, advice given, reactions and follow-ups.
Promotion record
Goal, dates, offer and results.
Returns record
Product returned, reason, refund or replacement and who agreed.

blocks.note: Clients' purchases are personal information. Keep records accurate, up to date and private; never share a client's details without her permission.
blocks.label: Jamaica

ul: Share what you learn about products and what clients ask for.
Pass a client to the right colleague, and give credit where it is due.
Keep the reception and the display tidy: it is everyone's job.
Tell the supervisor when stock is low, damaged or out of date, so it is ordered or removed in time.
I can tell retail products from professional (back-bar) products and say where to find correct product facts.
I can read a label: directions, ingredients, expiry date, open-jar symbol, SPF and warnings.
I can explain a feature and the benefit it brings, in plain words.
I can greet a client and build rapport, using open questions and listening.
I can check her record, ask about allergies, and judge her hair, skin or nail needs.
I can spot buying signals.
I can recommend one or two suitable products and explain why.
I can link a product or service to the one the client is having, and say what upselling is.
I can explain packages, bundles, discounts and free offers, and work out the price in J$.
I can let a client try a tester hygienically.
I can set up and keep a clean, safe, priced retail display.
I can plan and run a simple, honest promotion.
I can handle a price worry or other objection politely, without pressure.
I can close a sale politely and tell the client how to use and store the product.
I can follow up as agreed and note purchases on the record card.
I can sell without false claims, show prices, give receipts and handle a return fairly.
I can protect a client with allergies and explain why a patch test is needed.
I can record sales, work out progress against a target and explain commission.

blocks.note: In essay answers, give the reason for each step. For example: 'I ask open questions and listen first, so that I recommend what she needs and not what I want to sell.'
blocks.label: Tip

A product sold to clients for use at home.
Professional (back-bar) product
A product staff use on clients during services.

Buying signal
Something a client says or does that shows she wants to buy.
Link selling
Suggesting an item that goes with what the client is having.
Upselling
Offering a better or larger version of what the client is buying.
Package deal
Several services sold together for less than separately.
Bundle
Products sold together at one price.
Tester

Objection

Closing the sale

c1.title: Dry ends in Portmore
c1.text: Kayla Brown, 29, has just had a relaxer touch-up at a salon in Portmore. Her ends are dry and she tells trainee Shanique that her hair keeps breaking when she combs it. Shanique looks at Kayla's record card, which shows she has bought a heavy hair grease before. Shanique wants to recommend products for home care. She has a conditioner for chemically treated hair at J$2,400 and a tub tester of leave-in cream on the display.

c2.title: A pedicure and a price worry in Mandeville
c2.text: Mrs Beverley Walker is booked for a pedicure at a day spa in Mandeville. Her heels are dry and cracked. Therapist Dwayne suggests adding a paraffin wax heel treatment and a foot cream. Mrs Walker likes the idea but says the foot cream at J$3,200 is too dear this month. The spa has a smaller size of the same cream at J$1,800, and a free sample sachet.

c3.title: A body butter and an allergy in Ocho Rios
c3.text: At a spa in Ocho Rios, a client, Ms Tanya Francis, asks to buy a body butter after her massage. She mentions she is allergic to nuts. Trainee Omar has read the label, which lists shea butter, almond oil and coconut oil. A colleague tells him it is the best seller and to just sell it.

c4.title: A slow-selling scrub and a display in Kingston
c4.text: A day spa in New Kingston has 30 jars of body scrub that are selling slowly, with expiry dates in five months. The manager asks the staff to set up a display near reception and run a four-week promotion. The only free space is the window ledge facing the afternoon sun, beside the door. A trainee suggests letting clients dip their fingers into an open tub for a tester.

c5.title: A target month in Spanish Town
c5.text: Trainee stylist Tanisha has a monthly target of J$30,000 in product sales. With three days left she has sold J$22,500. Her supervisor has noticed she has started to push expensive products on every client, including a client who said her budget was tight. The salon pays 5% commission on product sales.

questions.q: What should Shanique do first, before recommending a product?
o: Ask open questions about how Kayla styles and cares for her hair
Show Kayla the conditioner and tell her its price
Explain that the grease she bought before was the wrong choice
Offer the leave-in tester and ask whether she likes the smell
questions.why: Find the need before you recommend. Open questions about styling, heat and home care show why the hair breaks, so the advice fits Kayla. Starting with a product or a criticism skips that step.

questions.q: Kayla says 'My ends are dry and they break.' Which is a benefit statement for the conditioner?
o: It is a J$2,400 bottle made by a well-known maker
It has a pump top and holds about 400 ml
It is made for chemically treated hair
It keeps your ends soft, so you will see less breakage
questions.why: A benefit says what the product does for this client. 'Soft ends, less breakage' answers Kayla's worry. The others are facts about the bottle: its price, size and type, which are features.

questions.q: Shanique wants Kayla to try the leave-in cream from the display tub. What is the hygienic way to do it?
o: Let Kayla dip a clean finger into the tub and rub it on her ends
Use a clean single-use spatula to place a little on her hand
Scoop some with a spoon from the staff room and wipe it afterwards
Tell her to smell the tub, since touching a tester is never allowed
questions.why: Many people use a tester, so it must stay clean: use a pump or a fresh single-use spatula each time, and never dip fingers or double-dip. Ask about allergies before it touches the skin.

questions.q: Kayla picks up the conditioner, reads the label, and asks how long a bottle lasts. What is this?
o: An objection to the price
A buying signal
A refusal to buy
A request for a discount
questions.why: Handling the product and asking how long it lasts show she is interested in owning it. Stop explaining and move towards closing the sale, for example by offering to put it with her bill.

questions.q: What is Dwayne's suggestion of the wax heel treatment and foot cream called?
o: Link selling, because they go with the service she is having
Upselling, because the foot cream replaces the pedicure she is having
A package deal, because the two items are priced together as one offer
A closing question, because it asks the client for payment straight away
questions.why: Link selling suggests items that go with the service the client is already having: for a pedicure, a foot treatment and foot cream. Upselling would offer a bigger or better version of the same thing.

questions.q: Mrs Walker says the J$3,200 cream is too dear this month. What is the best reply?
o: Agree that it is dear, then drop the idea and finish her pedicure quietly
Explain how long the jar lasts and show the smaller J$1,800 size
Tell her the offer ends today, so she should buy it now
Tell her the cheaper creams in the shops are not as good
questions.why: An objection is a concern to answer honestly: explain the value (how long it lasts) and offer a choice such as a smaller size or a sample. False urgency and running down other products are pressure, not advice.

questions.q: Mrs Walker still does not want to buy today. What should Dwayne do?
o: Remind her once more that the cream will improve her heels
Say the smaller size is the last one in stock
Give her the sample, accept her answer and note her interest
Add the cream to her bill and let her return it later if she changes her mind
questions.why: Accept a 'no' politely, give the sample so she can try it, and note her interest so you can mention it on her next visit. Pushing again, a false 'last one' claim or adding it to the bill without her agreement are unfair selling.

questions.q: The spa's 'Foot Care Package' is a pedicure at J$4,000 and a wax heel treatment at J$3,000, sold together for J$6,200. How much does Mrs Walker save?
questions.why: Add the separate prices: J$4,000 + J$3,000 = J$7,000. Subtract the package price: J$7,000 - J$6,200 = J$800 saved.

questions.q: What should Omar do first before selling the body butter to Ms Francis?
o: Read the ingredients for nut oils, as she is allergic to nuts
Ask his colleague whether other clients have had a reaction
Tell her the butter is so popular that it is bound to suit her
Let her try the tester on her arm, since a small patch will show quickly
questions.why: The label shows almond oil, a nut oil, so the product is unsuitable for a client with a nut allergy. Always read the ingredients before you sell or apply a product to someone who has told you about an allergy; do not test it on her skin.

questions.q: What is the best way for Omar to help Ms Francis?
o: Sell it anyway and tell her to stop using it if her skin starts to itch
Explain the ingredient, say it is not suitable, and offer a nut-free product
Tell her that almond oil is too mild to cause a reaction in most people
Hide the label and tell her that it is only made with coconut oil
questions.why: Being honest protects the client and the salon. Explain why the product is not suitable and offer one that suits her. Hiding information or downplaying an allergy puts her at risk and is dishonest selling.

questions.q: A colleague tells Omar to 'just sell it'. What does honest selling require?
o: Selling whatever is the best seller, since that makes the salon most money
Following the client's needs and the facts, not pressure from a colleague
Doing what the senior colleague says, since she has been there longer
Selling the product but asking the client to sign that she was warned
questions.why: The client's needs, safety and the true facts come first. A colleague's instruction does not make an unsuitable sale acceptable. If you are unsure, tell your supervisor.

questions.q: Why is the window ledge facing the afternoon sun a poor place for the scrub display?
o: Clients cannot see products in a window from the street
Heat and sunlight can spoil the products and fade the labels
A window ledge is too narrow to hold more than a few jars
Direct sun makes products look dull, so clients do not notice them
questions.why: Direct sun and heat can make creams and scrubs separate or spoil and can fade labels, which matters in Jamaica's heat. Choose a place clear of sun, walkways and the fire exit, such as near reception.

questions.q: What should the staff do about the tester for the body scrub?
o: Let clients dip their fingers into an open tub, as a spa is a clean place
Put out a tester tub and wipe its surface with a tissue between clients
Offer a pump bottle, or a fresh single-use spatula with a marked tester tub
Skip the tester, because a client should buy it without trying it first
questions.why: Testers must be hygienic: a pump, or a fresh single-use spatula for a tub, clearly marked, with allergy questions first. Fingers in a shared tub spread germs, and wiping does not make it clean.

questions.q: Which is the fairest, most honest promotion for the scrub jars?
o: Mark the jars 'last chance' and double the old price to show a big saving
Offer a small discount with a clear sign giving the price and the end date
Move the oldest jars to the back and sell the newest first
Tell clients the scrub will help any skin condition they have
questions.why: A fair promotion shows the real price, the offer and the end date. False 'last chance' claims, an inflated 'was' price and health claims are unfair selling. Older stock should be sold first (first in, first out), not hidden.

questions.q: Tanisha has J$22,500 of her J$30,000 target, with three days left. How much more must she sell to reach it?
What is wrong with the way Tanisha has started selling?
o: She is selling more than the target, which is unfair to her co-workers
She is pushing products whatever the need, so clients feel pressured
She is offering clients samples to try, which is a waste of the stock
She is writing purchases on record cards, which should stay private
questions.why: Selling by need, not by target, builds trust. Pushing expensive products on a client with a tight budget damages trust and can be unfair selling, even though a target can make it tempting.

questions.q: If Tanisha sells J$40,000 of products in a month and the salon pays 5% commission, how much commission does she earn?
questions.why: 5% of J$40,000 = J$40,000 x 5 / 100 = J$2,000. Commission is an extra payment, usually a part of sales.

questions.q: A client asks whether a cream will remove her stretch marks completely. The maker claims only that it 'helps skin feel softer'. What should you say?
o: Yes, it will clear them if she uses it every day for a month
It may help your skin feel softer, but it will not remove them
No cream can help, so there is no reason to buy it
I am not sure; buy it and see what happens
questions.why: Say only what the maker truthfully claims. A false promise misleads the client and breaks the rules on honest selling; a flat 'no cream helps' is also untrue.

questions.q: Which of these is an open question that helps you find out a client's needs?
o: Do you like this shampoo?
Is your hair dry?
How do you care for your skin at home?
Would you like to buy the large size?
questions.why: An open question starts with how, what or why and gets the client talking about her needs. The others can be answered with a yes or no, or move to the sale too early.

questions.q: A client bought a shampoo and brings it back with her receipt, saying it was spoiled when she opened it. What is the correct first response?
o: Tell her that all sales are final once the seal has been broken on it
Listen, apologise, check receipt and product, and follow the returns policy
Give her the cash straight away without checking anything, just to keep her happy
Ask her to come back another day when the owner is in the salon and not busy
questions.why: A client has the right to a fair remedy for a faulty product. Listen, apologise, check the receipt and the product, then follow the salon's policy with a supervisor's agreement where needed.
